definition.text: A theory of how people actually make choices under risk, developed by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979.

facts.text: Unlike expected utility theory, which models what perfectly rational agents would do, it aims to describe real behavior.
People judge gains and losses relative to a reference point, their current situation, rather than by absolute wealth.
Losses are felt more sharply than equal gains: for some people the pain of losing $1,000 is only made up by the pleasure of gaining $2,000.
Its value function is concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses, so people avoid risk over gains and seek risk over losses.
Choices pass through an editing phase, where a reference point is set and outcomes are coded as gains or losses, before they are evaluated.
It was cited when Kahneman received the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, and Tversky and Kahneman's work largely launched behavioral economics.
Jeffrey Berejikian used it to analyse how the Montreal Protocol, a landmark environmental agreement, came about.
Critics note that the reference point is hard to pin down, since many outside factors shape what counts as a gain or a loss.

definition.text: The tendency, derived from prospect theory, to focus on short-term gains and losses and weigh them more heavily than long-term ones.

facts.text: It can lead people to avoid immediate losses at the expense of long-term gains.
In a 1997 betting study by Gneezy and Potters, players bet more after losing a round and less after winning one, rather than looking at total earnings.

definition.text: A revised version of prospect theory that weights probabilities by rank, fixing flaws in the original version.

facts.text: The original version could prefer one prospect over another even when the other was at least as good at every outcome level, violating first-order stochastic dominance.
The cumulative version borrows its probability weighting from rank-dependent expected utility theory and also works for continuous outcomes.

definition.text: A standard economics experiment in which players secretly decide how many of their tokens to put into a shared pot that is multiplied and split among everyone.

facts.text: Each player's payoff is what they kept plus their share of the multiplied pot, so it is used to study altruism, cooperation and free riding.
If players are purely selfish, the Nash equilibrium is that nobody contributes.
It tests the theory that public goods, such as street lighting that no one can be excluded from, are under-provided because no one has a private motive to pay.
In repeated play contributions usually decline as generous players see others give less, but they rarely reach zero because a hard core of givers remains.
Players will punish non-contributors even at a cost to themselves, and in most experiments this raises group cooperation.
With 40 players, a multiplier of 1.03 leads almost everyone to stop giving, while a multiplier of 1.3 keeps average contributions around 50%.
Framing the same game as a climate negotiation rather than neutrally can change how players behave.
Contributions tend to be lower when players start with unequal endowments.
